standard.title: Spelling for stylistic effect
standard.description: understand how spelling is used in texts for particular effects; for example, characterisation, humour and to represent accents and distinctive speech
standard.prior_knowledge: Students use spelling rules and word origins including Greek and Latin roots to learn and spell new words (AC9E7LY08). They have not yet examined spelling as a deliberate authorial device used for characterisation, humour and accent representation.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students understand how spelling is used deliberately in texts to create effects including characterisation, humour and representation of accents and distinctive speech.

nodes.label: Spelling as characterisation device
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify deliberate spelling variations used to represent character speech and explain the characterisation effect they create.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least one example where an author has varied spelling to represent a character's speech and explain what the variation reveals about the character.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse how authors drop letters or use non-standard spelling to emulate the sound of spoken words, examining what the spelling choices contribute to characterisation — accent, dialect, education level, personality.
wider: Compare how different authors represent similar accents through spelling — examining the range of conventions and what is gained or risked by each approach
Examine the ethics of using non-standard spelling to represent a character's speech, considering who makes such choices and what effects they have on readers from that community

response_modes.reason: The intent-versus-error distinction is the central challenge here — students need to see that deliberate spelling variation is an authorial choice, not a mistake. Multiple author examples across genres and character types help resolve this.

success_criteria: Student identifies a deliberate spelling variation and names the characterisation effect it creates
Student explains how the spelling variation represents spoken features (accent, dialect, distinctiveness) that standard spelling would mask

nodes.label: Spelling for humour and neologism
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify how unconventional spelling is used in media texts for humour or to create neologisms, and explain the effect.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify a neologism or humorous spelling in a media text and explain what effect the unconventional spelling creates.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse how spelling is used in media texts such as online posts for humour and neologism creation — examining how spelling variation signals register, in-group knowledge and cultural currency.
wider: Trace how a digital neologism ('selfie', 'binge-watch', 'photobomb') entered mainstream usage, examining how its spelling and form stabilised or shifted
Compare how intentional misspelling functions in advertising versus social media — examining what different communities accept and why

response_modes.reason: Neologism and humorous spelling are most visible in digital and media texts that students already encounter. Seeing multiple examples across online posts, advertising and social media — where spelling deviation is normalised for different purposes — builds the analytical habit of asking what the non-standard spelling is doing, not just noting it.

success_criteria: Student identifies a spelling effect (humour, neologism, accent) and names what creates it
Student explains how the unconventional spelling generates its effect — why it works rather than just noting that it does
